transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-12-05
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Derek Sosa (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Voltaic Head of Platform), Liam O'Connor (Voltaic InfoSec), Rashid Khan (Voltaic Network Eng), Nora Liu (Voltaic ML)

Summary:
Brief discovery focused on private/VPC onramp options for Voltaic's inference traffic. Key topics: egress IPs and allowlisting, Transit Gateway vs direct VPC peering, multi-region constraints (EU data residency), KMS/HSM integration, SOC2/audit expectations, pilot scope and success criteria.

Topics:
- Connectivity modes: PrivateLink/private endpoints vs Transit Gateway peering
- Egress and fixed IP ranges
- Cross-region routing and data residency (EU and APAC gating)
- KMS/HSM and encryption at rest/in flight
- Pilot: performance benchmarks and throughput profile

Action items noted in metadata above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood. We'll keep this to about 45 minutes and focus on your private onramp questions. Quick intros?
[00:12] Aisha Patel: Hi, Aisha here, Head of Platform at Voltaic. We've got a shortlist of things - we need predictable egress addresses, SOC2 controls, and EU-only routing for certain models.
[00:22] Liam O'Connor: Liam, InfoSec. My main concerns are auditability, key management (we run AWS KMS + HSM), and ensuring no data egress to third-party regions.
[00:30] Derek Sosa: Great, Derek from Redwood SE. We work a lot on Transit Gateway and PrivateLink patterns. We'll try to map out options you can choose from.
[00:36] Rashid Khan: Rashid, network. Our infra is hybrid — primary on AWS, some GCP for analytics. We use a TGW hub-and-spoke model and also have a managed firewall that requires static egress IP ranges.
[00:47] Maya Chen: Perfect. High level, Redwood supports three deployment modes — hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, and private (VPC/private control plane). Today sounds like private is most likely?
[00:56] Aisha Patel: Yeah leaning private. We can't send certain EU customer PII outside the region, and we want to own the networking endpoint.
[01:06] Priya Rao: Quick clarification: when you say "own the endpoint", do you mean you want a VPC endpoint in your account that talks to Redwood compute in your region, or do you want us to host compute inside your VPC?
[01:17] Nora Liu: We prefer Redwood-managed compute but accessible only via our VPC — basically PrivateLink or Private Endpoint into Redwood's service. We want the control plane to be private too if possible.
[01:27] Derek Sosa: OK, that's our Private deployment pattern: a private control plane that reaches into your VPC via PrivateLink (AWS) or private endpoint equivalents. For dedicated/private offerings we can also do customer-managed VPC peering or colocated private agents, depending on compliance.
[01:42] Rashid Khan: What's the difference between PrivateLink and peering here? Which gives us predictable egress IPs?
[01:49] Derek Sosa: Good question. PrivateLink provides an endpoint ENI in your VPC that talks to our service with AWS-managed connectivity; egress will look like it comes from the endpoint's subnet/ENI. For peering/TGW, traffic routes across the peering and egress may be from our side unless you front with a NAT gateway. The deterministic IPs are easiest with NAT + EIP on your side or with static outbound IPs from a dedicated Redwood egress appliance if you choose dedicated.
[02:12] Liam O'Connor: So if we require a single small set of public IPs to allowlist, what's the recommended approach? We can't maintain huge IP ranges.
[02:22] Maya Chen: For Hosted customers, we publish regional IP ranges — but they are larger. For Private/Dedicated we can offer a small fixed set of egress IPs per region. Typically that's in a dedicated deployment or via a managed NAT we provide alongside the private plane. We'll follow up with an allowlist template.
[02:40] Aisha Patel: And for data residency — we need EU-bound requests to never leave eu-west-1. Can Redwood enforce that?
[02:49] Priya Rao: Yes, with per-customer routing policies and region pinning. We can provision model serving inside eu-west-1 and enforce routing at the control plane. If you use multi-region failover, we'll agree on fallback rules — default is no cross-region unless you opt in.
[03:05] Rashid Khan: What about GCP? We have analytics on GCP in europe-west2, could we peer to Redwood via Interconnect?
[03:13] Derek Sosa: We support peering patterns for GCP too. For private connectivity in GCP you'd use a VPC peering or Private Service Connect. We can work with your cloud provider network team. The important piece is shared CIDR planning and ensuring no overlapping subnets.
[03:28] Liam O'Connor: KMS/hsm integration — we use an external HSM provider via AWS CloudHSM. Do you support customer-managed keys for model artifact encryption and logs?
[03:38] Maya Chen: Yes, we support BYOK patterns. For Private deployments we can integrate with your KMS/HSM for at-rest encryption. For Hosted we have options too but in Private you have direct KMS control. We'll capture the key rotation and access model in the security docs.
[03:53] Nora Liu: Is there any performance impact when KMS calls are made per request? Our inference path is latency sensitive.
[04:00] Derek Sosa: We only use KMS for key wrapping and envelope encryption at start/periodically — not per token. Latency-sensitive paths use the wrapped data keys cached on the host. So negligible per-request latency.
[04:12] Aisha Patel: Ok that's good. Our next question — throughput. We expect about 1k QPS peak for token-generation workloads with a mix of 16-64 token responses. Any guidance on instance sizing?
[04:23] Derek Sosa: We'll need a benchmark with your exact prompt mix. Roughly, for autoregressive models we recommend dedicated GPU pools — M-profile or H-profile depending on quantization. For 1k QPS you may want an initial Dedicated pool plus autoscale to handle bursts. I'll capture rough vGPU counts in the follow-up.
[04:41] Rashid Khan: Network-wise, we have a firewall that requires short TTLs on peering routes and we do IP slicing for multi-tenant racks — is that a problem for PrivateLink?
[04:52] Derek Sosa: PrivateLink uses endpoint ENIs in your subnets, so as long as routing/ACLs allow the ENI and security groups, it should be fine. For TGW-based routing with IP slicing we need to ensure route propagation matches your NAT/firewall expectations. We occasionally see routes getting stripped in aggressive ACLs — typically solved by an allow rule for the Redwood endpoint subnets.
[05:12] Liam O'Connor: Audit logging — we need per-request logs for compliance and a tamper-evident trail. Can Redwood push audit logs to our S3/Azure Blob or SIEM?
[05:22] Priya Rao: Yes, for Private deployments we can forward audit logs (requests metadata, response hashes) to your logging bucket or SIEM via secure transfer. Full payload logs we generally don't forward unless contracted due to privacy, but we can provide metadata and hashes.
[05:36] Aisha Patel: Hashes are fine; we want to be able to trace which model version served an inference for audit.
[05:42] Maya Chen: We support model version tagging and per-request model id in the audit log.
[05:48] Rashid Khan: Let's talk NAT and egress. If you're providing a small set of egress IPs from Redwood, what happens during failover or upgrades? Will IPs change?
[05:58] Derek Sosa: In Dedicated setups we can allocate static EIPs that are stable across upgrades. In multi-AZ failover, we use floating IPs or BGP announcements to keep egress stable. For Hosted, ranges can shift — that's why we recommend Private/Dedicated if you need stable allowlist addresses.
[06:16] Liam O'Connor: Let's say we want to use our own NAT with fixed EIP. Can we route outgoing traffic through our NAT so the destination sees our EIP?
[06:25] Maya Chen: Yes, we support customer-side NAT. In that case, outbound from Redwood to external services goes through your NAT; so the external world always sees your EIP. That is commonly used when customers want the final egress control.
[06:39] Nora Liu: Any limits on subnet sizes or route table entries? Our TGW already has a lot of routes.
[06:46] Derek Sosa: We recommend planning for /24s for endpoint ENIs to avoid overlap; route table limits differ by provider, but we try to minimize required static routes by using service endpoints or TGW attachments instead of individual peering per subnet. We'll work with your network team to map exactly.
[07:02] Aisha Patel: On the security front: SSO, RBAC, SCIM provisioning — supported?
[07:07] Priya Rao: Yes — SAML SSO, SCIM for user provisioning, and RBAC with token-scoped permissions are all supported. In Private you can also enforce IP-based controls and restrict token scopes at the tenant level.
[07:20] Liam O'Connor: Do you have SOC 2 Type II and ISO? Also penetration testing policies?
[07:25] Maya Chen: We have SOC 2 Type II. We'll share the security pack. We also do annual pen tests and can provide scoping for a customer-led red/blue test for Private deployments.
[07:37] Rashid Khan: For the pilot, we want to validate throughput and egress behaviors plus EU-only routing. What should success criteria look like?
[07:46] Derek Sosa: Typical pilot success criteria: 1) Achieve expected QPS with P95 latency targets, 2) egress IPs stable and allowlisting verified, 3) audit logs delivered to your SIEM, 4) KMS integration validated, and 5) no cross-region leakage for EU traffic.
[08:02] Nora Liu: Timeline wise — we want pilot in the next two weeks. Is that realistic?
[08:07] Maya Chen: We can scope a light pilot in two weeks if we get the VPC CIDR and allowlist info this week. Derek, is that doable?
[08:13] Derek Sosa: Yes, I'll need CIDRs, firewall rules, and a contact for a network peer. We can also run an isolated throughput bench with sample prompts once connectivity is established.
[08:25] Aisha Patel: On pricing — what's the difference cost-wise between Dedicated and Private? We need a ballpark for budgeting.
[08:31] Maya Chen: Dedicated is typically a reserved capacity model with committed monthly spend and lower per-token/unit cost. Private has platform licensing + optional reserved capacity. I'll send indicative numbers but we'll tailor based on throughput and retention.
[08:44] Liam O'Connor: Competitors — we've evaluated Anthropic and OpenAI's hosted offerings, but those don't meet our EU-gating + KMS requirements easily. Also internally we considered self-hosting but that's 6–9 months of infra work.
[08:58] Priya Rao: One operational note — we can provide a small sandbox in eu-west-1 for initial connectivity testing so you can verify route tables and egress without touching prod.
[09:09] Rashid Khan: That sandbox would be perfect. We'll need the endpoint ENI subnet range to pre-provision security groups.
[09:16] Derek Sosa: We'll include the subnet suggestion in the allowlist template.
[09:20] Aisha Patel: Any gotchas on DNS? We use strict DNS filtering and split-horizon DNS.
[09:26] Maya Chen: For PrivateLink we recommend using private hosted zones mapped to the PrivateLink endpoint; DNS must resolve the service to the endpoint ENI. If you have split-horizon, we'll provide the private DNS name and guidance for your resolver team.
[09:39] Liam O'Connor: About encryption in flight — do you terminate TLS at the endpoint? We insist on mutual TLS for critical flows.
[09:46] Priya Rao: We support mTLS between customer and Redwood in Private setups. We can also use client certs + SNI. For API calls we support TLS 1.3 and mutual auth where required.
[09:57] Rashid Khan: If we do a failover from eu-west-1 to another EU region, will the IPs change? We cannot change allowlists mid-contract.
[10:05] Derek Sosa: Failover IP stability depends on the deployment plan. If you need invariant IPs across failover, dedicated EIPs with anycast/BGP are options but add complexity. Alternatively, we can design a regional-only failover policy within the same region.
[10:18] Maya Chen: Sounds like we need to document acceptable failover behavior in the SLA. We'll propose options.
[10:24] Aisha Patel: Also, not sure if you support evacuation windows for maintenance where we can drain traffic first.
[10:30] Derek Sosa: We do rolling upgrades and can coordinate maintenance windows. For dedicated pools we can schedule no-upgrade windows during your peak times if contracted.
[10:40] Nora Liu: Regarding telemetry: do you expose per-token cost and per-route latency breakdowns? That's important for our FinOps team.
[10:47] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Console has token-level cost and latency breakdown per model/route. We can grant read-only access to your FinOps.
[10:55] Rashid Khan: On peering specifics — what about overlapping subnets? We have some legacy /16s that conflict.
[11:01] Derek Sosa: Overlap is a blocker for peering. We can work around with NAT or proxying, but best to reassign the overlapping ranges for the private endpoint. For TGW we can sometimes use route translation but that's complex.
[11:13] Aisha Patel: Let's talk immediate next steps to get the pilot greenlit.
[11:18] Maya Chen: We'll: 1) send the private-connectivity checklist and allowlist template, 2) share SOC2 snapshot and security whitepaper, 3) schedule a SE-led connectivity workshop with your network team next week, and 4) provide indicative pricing for Dedicated vs Private pilot.
[11:33] Rashid Khan: I'll collect the CIDRs and firewall rules and share them by Dec 8.
[11:38] Liam O'Connor: I'll review the SOC2 docs once you send them. Also want to confirm pen-test arrangements in contract.
[11:45] Maya Chen: Noted — we'll include pen-test scope and vendor expectations.
[11:49] Priya Rao: Derek and I will prep throughput notes and a proposed bench plan for your 1k QPS case.
[11:56] Aisha Patel: Great. Any final questions?
[11:59] Nora Liu: Just one: for the sandbox bench, will you provide sample model images or do we need to bring our prompts?
[12:05] Derek Sosa: We'll provide a small set of representative prompts and you can run your own too. The bench will include both to mirror realistic latency.
[12:13] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule. Appreciate the time.
[12:18] Aisha Patel: Thanks everyone.
[12:20] End of call.

Notes about transcription: occasional words misheard — "Transit Gateway" sometimes transcribed as "Transit Toby" in auto captions; "KV cache" appears as "K-B cache" in earlier auto notes. We left those as-is in places where the auto-transcript produced them.
